Install docker with convenience script

Fine for learning and test environments, but not recommended by Docker for production systems (use the apt repository there)

Post installation step: Add your user (eg. ubuntu) to the docker group, so you can run docker without sudo

sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu
newgrp docker

Which terminal should I use? (Windows)
Use PowerShell (e.g. the VS Code terminal) for all exercises. Docker Desktop must be running.
If you use Git Bash instead, two things go wrong:

docker run -it ... and docker exec -it ... fail with the input device is not a TTY. Fix: put winpty in front of the command, e.g. winpty docker run -it ubuntu bash.
Paths like /bin/bash are converted into Windows paths. Fix: write bash instead of /bin/bash, or write //bin/bash.

title: Docker
text:
Docker Terms



Term
Description
Main commands




Docker Image
A read-only template which contains everything needed to run an application as a container. Consists of several layers.
docker images lists all images available in the local image cache (pulled or built before).


Docker Container
A single runtime instance of a docker image. From one image, a lot of containers can be started and stopped, with individual execution parameters (e.g. for the port mapping of a container).
docker ps lists all running docker containers
docker ps -a including stopped containers


Docker Registry
A registry stores and distributes docker images. Docker Hub is the default registry and hosts a huge number of public images including usage documentation and version histories. It can also be used for managing private docker images. Besides Docker Hub, there are a lot of other container registries, e.g. the GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io).
docker pull, docker push


Dockerfile
A text file containing commands for building a new docker image. Instructions that change the file system (like RUN and COPY) each add a new image layer. Dockerfile syntax uses instructions like FROM for referring a base image, RUN for executing a shell command, COPY for copying files from the local file system into the image, and CMD for specifying the start command of the application which will be executed whenever a container from that image is started.
docker build -t <image-name> .


Docker Compose
A tool for defining and running multi-container applications in a YAML file
docker compose up
docker compose down

Troubleshooting



Error message
Cause
Fix




Cannot connect to the Docker daemon / error during connect
Docker Desktop is not running
Start Docker Desktop and wait until it says “Engine running”


the input device is not a TTY
You use Git Bash
Use PowerShell, or put winpty in front of the command (see above)


port is already allocated / address already in use
Another container (or program) already uses this host port
docker ps → remove the old container, or choose another host port (left side of -p)


The container name "/..." is already in use
A container with this name still exists (maybe stopped)
docker rm -f <name>, or docker compose down in the folder of the other exercise

A local program (e.g. XAMPP MySQL/Apache) uses the port
Stop that program, or use another host port


Browser shows nothing / “connection refused”
Wrong port, or the container has stopped
Check the PORTS column in docker ps; check docker logs <name>

title: 1  Container commands
text: 1.1 Interactive container

title: 1  Container commands
text:
docker run --name helloDocker -i -t ubuntu /bin/bash
           |                  |  |  |      |
           |                  |  |  |      +-- Command to run
           |                  |  |  +--------- Image to start the container from
           |                  |  +------------ Allocate a pseudo-TTY
           |                  +--------------- Keep STDIN open (-i -t is usually written as -it)
           +---------------------------------- Name of container

1.1.1 Exercise:

Run this command => ubuntu image will be downloaded to the local image cache and a bash prompt is opened.
Inspect the running ubuntu instance via the bash terminal, for example:

hostname - which name does the container have?
cat /etc/os-release - which Linux version is running inside?
ps aux - which processes are running? (only very few - compare with your own computer!)
ls / - the container has its own file system

Use another terminal to inspect

the running docker instance with docker ps - note the container id is the same as displayed in the bash prompt => by default, the (short) container id is used as the host name of the container.
docker images will display the downloaded ubuntu image.

Exit the container instance with typing exit in the bash prompt.

This also stops the container: a container only runs as long as its main process (here: bash) runs.
Use docker ps -a to list all containers, including stopped ones.
Use docker start <container-id> to restart the stopped container. You can see it now running again with docker ps, however you are not connected with the bash terminal.
Use docker attach <container-id> to attach your terminal to the bash prompt again.

title: 1  Container commands
text:
1.2 Background process
docker run -d ubuntu /bin/bash -c "while true; do echo hello world; sleep 1; done"
           |
           +---- Detached (= background server process)

1.2.1 Exercise:

Inspect the running container with docker ps => note the container-id.
Use docker logs <container-id> to view the output of the bash command that is running in the container.
Use docker stop <container-id> to stop this container.
Use docker ps -a to list the stopped container as well as all other running containers.
Use docker rm <container-id> to remove the stopped container.



1.2.2 Notes

It is sufficient to enter only the first few characters of the container id - as long as this prefix is unique and docker is thus able to identify the container.
You can remove a still running container by using the force option: docker rm -f <container-id>.

title: 1  Container commands
text:
1.3 Nginx Webserver
docker container run is the long form of docker run - both commands do the same.
docker container run -d -p 8080:80 --name my-webserver nginx
                     |  |          |                   |
                     |  |          |                   +------- Image, from which the container is started
                     |  |          +--------------------------- Option to specify the container name
                     |  +-------------------------------------- Publish container port 80 (where nginx listens)
                     |                                          on port 8080 of the host
                     +----------------------------------------- detached mode (running in background)

1.3.1 Exercise

Run this command
List the container with docker ps: It should display

the correct port mapping from the host port 8080 to the container port 80
as well as the image nginx
and the requested container name my-webserver 

Check your image cache with docker images (nginx image should have been pulled from Docker Hub)
Connect to the web service from your favourite browser via http://localhost:8080. It should display the default index.html for nginx: 
Check the logging of your client connection with docker logs my-webserver (we can now use the container name instead of the container-id)
Check the processes running inside this container with docker top my-webserver
Stop and restart the web service with docker stop and docker start
Stop the web service again with docker stop my-webserver, then remove it with docker rm my-webserver (docker rm refuses to remove a running container)

title: 1  Container commands
text:
1.4 Bind Mounts
For publishing a local html folder in your nginx container, you need to specify a bind mount with the -v option (alternatively: --mount type=bind,source=...,target=...):

Note the colon : between the local folder and the folder inside the container!
If your local folder looks like following, your web browser will display your individual index.html file after connecting to this new web service:
C
+- htl
   +- docker
      +- wwwroot
         +- index.html
The command from the picture, to copy (with port 8081, so it does not collide with my-webserver from above):
docker run -d -p 8081:80 -v C:/htl/docker/wwwroot:/usr/share/nginx/html --name my-bind-webserver nginx
Tip: This repository already contains a folder 01-containers/wwwroot with an index.html. If you open a PowerShell terminal in the 01-containers folder, you can use it with ${PWD} (= current folder):
docker run -d -p 8081:80 -v ${PWD}/wwwroot:/usr/share/nginx/html --name my-bind-webserver nginx
(On Linux / macOS, write $(pwd) instead of ${PWD}.)

1.4.1 Exercise:

Create folder structure + index.html file (or use the wwwroot folder of this repository)
Start a new container with a bind mount and a new port mapping - e.g. with 8081 instead of 8080
Contact this web service with your favourite browser: http://localhost:8081 should show your index.html, not the nginx default page
Use docker inspect to inspect the properties of the new container
Use docker stats to inspect the performance statistics
Use docker logs to access the web server log messages
Use docker exec -it <id> bash to connect to the container in interactive tty mode with a bash terminal. Navigate to the /usr/share/nginx/html folder to inspect the mounted files.
Edit the index.html file on your host file system, save it and refresh your browser to see the changed content.
Add additional files to the mounted folder and check, if they are reachable via your web browser.
Clean up: docker rm -f my-bind-webserver

title: 2  Docker Images
text:
2.3 Create Image from a Container
Unusual, but possible: Modify a container and save it to a new image.

2.3.1 Step 1: Nginx with Live-Editing
Instead of mapping a local folder into an nginx container, we could also edit the index.html file inside the container by means of a linux editor like nano.

Start a plain nginx container: docker run -p 8082:80 -d --name editable-webserver nginx
Execute a bash terminal in the container: docker exec -it editable-webserver bash
Navigate to the folder containing the index.html: cd /usr/share/nginx/html
Try to edit this file: nano index.html

nano is not installed in the very slim base image for nginx, hence we need to install it first …
cat or more would be available, but this doesn’t help

Install nano:

First, package lists must be updated, since the base image doesn’t contain any: apt update
Next, we can install nano: apt install nano.
Note that apt install asks for confirmation. Auto-answer with yes with the option -y: apt install -y nano

Now edit index.html with nano, save the changes and reload the page in the browser.



2.3.2 Step 2: Save modified container to image
For each new container started from the base image nginx, those changes would be lost. But we can store the modifications done in the container to a new image layer:

Exit the container bash
Commit the container changes to a new image (docker commit): docker commit -m "change-description" <container-id> <image-name>

where image-name could be nginx-editable

Inspect the new image with docker images and note the difference in size compared to the original base image nginx, resulting from the nano package installed.



2.3.3 Step 3: Start a new container

Run a new container from the new image: docker run -p 8083:80 -d nginx-editable
Test it on port 8083

You should see the modified index.html
If executing a bash inside the new container, you can use nano to edit files

title: 2  Docker Images
text:
2.4 Dockerfile
The most common way to build an image is using a Dockerfile. See the Dockerfile reference.

2.4.1 Dockerfile Syntax








Instruction
Description
Example




FROM
A new image is always built based on another image, at minimum FROM scratch. This reference image will be extended with the given Dockerfile
FROM nginx


RUN
One or more shell commands to be executed while building the image. Referring to the previous example, we could do the package update and install commands here. Since each RUN statement results in a distinct image layer, we can save effort by combining several commands with &&. In Dockerfiles, apt-get is preferred over apt, since apt is meant for interactive use.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nano


WORKDIR
Sets the working directory for all subsequent instructions (and for the running container). If the folder does not yet exist, it will be created.
WORKDIR /usr/share/nginx/html


COPY
To make specific files or folder appear in a future container of the new image, they must be copied from the build context (the folder passed to docker build) into the image. For example, a prepared web root folder can be copied into the nginx html folder. Source paths are always relative to the build context, destination paths are relative to the WORKDIR of the image (unless absolute). So COPY . . copies the whole build context into the current working directory of the image.
COPY . .


EXPOSE
A Dockerfile might declare the container port on which the service will be listening after startup. This does not publish the port, it mainly serves as documentation. This is very useful for a successful port mapping in the docker run command, since the right part of a port mapping must refer to the container port.
EXPOSE 80 (e.g., for a typical web server)


CMD
Usually the last instruction in a Dockerfile, which specifies the default command to start the application. This command is executed each time a container of this image is started, unless another command is passed to docker run. The preferred exec form is written as JSON array.
CMD ["node", "app.js"] (for a node application)

title: 5  Javascript Express Backend
text:
5.1 Dockerfile
What do you need to build a simple node.js express backend service in your local development environment?
All those steps can be packaged into a docker image, so there is no local Node.js installation required anymore => the app can run wherever docker is installed.

title: 5  Javascript Express Backend
text:
FROM node:24 - Node.js is required. Always specify a version tag, otherwise you get whatever latest currently is.
WORKDIR /app - Creates a new folder where we will store the app including the node_modules
COPY . . - Copies app.js, package.json from the build context into the app folder of this image
RUN npm install - Creates package-lock.json and node_modules
EXPOSE 3000 - Declares that our express service will listen on container port 3000 after startup
CMD ["node", "app.js"] - Finally declares how to startup the express service

… you should know already how …

title: 5  Javascript Express Backend

title: 5  Javascript Express Backend
text:
5.5 Dockerignore
Note the file .dockerignore which excludes files matching the given rules from the build context, so COPY (and ADD) cannot copy them into the image.
Hence we can avoid that files like Readme.md and the Dockerfile itself will be copied to the image, since they are not needed for running the application. Even more important: a local node_modules folder is excluded too, so it cannot overwrite the dependencies installed by npm install inside the image.
Refer to https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/#dockerignore-files

title: 6  Multistage Dockerfiles
text:
6.1 Java EchoServer
This Java program launches a server listening on incoming connections on port 9001. It will answer with some greeting and then echoes all text communication which is sent from the client terminal.
What is relevant for dockerizing this service:

title: 6  Multistage Dockerfiles
text:
Internal port for the port mapping: 9001
How to compile a Java source file: javac compiler which is part of JDK
How to run the Java Bytecode file to launch the program: java which is part of the java runtime jre

title: 6  Multistage Dockerfiles
text:
6.2 Dockerfile
Since a full JDK environment is much larger than the java runtime itself, we save effort and file size by separating the image build process into two distinct stages (multi-stage build):

Build Stage for compiling the .class bytecode file from the .java source file
Run Stage for preparing the execution environment for launching the bytecode file with jre


6.2.1 Stage 1: Build Stage
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY EchoServer.java ./
RUN javac *.java
Note:

This build stage is named builder, so the next stage can refer to it.
The former openjdk images are deprecated on Docker Hub, eclipse-temurin is a recommended replacement.
This stage won’t be part of the final image after the docker build is complete => image file size is minimized.



6.2.2 Stage 2: Run Stage
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/EchoServer.class .
EXPOSE 9001
CMD ["java", "EchoServer"]
Notes:

Final image only requires jre environment
Bytecode file is copied from the previous build stage
EXPOSE 9001 documents the port the echo server listens on
Startup command calls the java program and passes the class name EchoServer (without the .class extension) as an argument.

title: 7  TypeScript Backend Dockerfile
text:
7.1 Fruits Rest-Api
Given is the already known sample for the Fruits Rest-Api with following changes:

title: 7  TypeScript Backend Dockerfile
text:
requests.http:

Introduced variable for HOSTNAME so we can edit the host name and port in a single place, if someone maps the container port to a different external port than 3000.

package.json:

added build script for the build stage
installed missing cors dependencies

tsconfig.json:

set outDir to dist folder so the js files will be transpiled into this folder.
Thus, we can keep the files required for launching the program in a separate folder, which makes copying easier.

title: 7  TypeScript Backend Dockerfile
text:
7.2 Dockerfile
A typescript app involves a compilation (transpilation) step, which needs the full node image including npm and the TypeScript compiler. For launching the transpiled app.js file, however, only the Node.js runtime is required. Google’s distroless images contain nothing but the runtime (no shell, no package manager), so the final image is only a fraction of the size of the full node image (check the difference with docker images).

Refer to: https://github.com/GoogleContainerTools/distroless

So it definitely makes sense to split the Dockerfile into two stages.

7.2.1 Step 1: Build Stage

FROM node:24 AS builder:

Full node image (including npm) for building
Write AS in upper case like FROM, otherwise docker build prints a FromAsCasing warning

WORKDIR /app:

We will install and transpile into this folder

COPY ./package*.json ./:

First, only copy package.json and package-lock.json (if present) from the build context into the image.
This reduces build time for later docker builds: docker caches each build step and reuses it, as long as the files copied in this step have not changed. So npm install only runs again if the dependencies changed.

RUN npm install:

creates node_modules in app folder

COPY . .:

Now, all the rest is copied from the build context into the image, including tsconfig.json and the ts source files.
The .dockerignore file makes sure that a local node_modules or dist folder is not copied, since it would overwrite the folders created inside the image.

RUN npm run build:

Javascript files are transpiled into /app/dist folder




7.2.2 Step 2: Run Stage

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian12

For running the javascript files, a small distroless image containing only the Node.js 24 runtime is used.

WORKDIR /app

Again, we define a common base folder for the program

COPY --from=builder /app/dist .

Copy js files

COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules

Copy js dependencies

EXPOSE 3000

Declare the port on which our express application listens

CMD ["app.js"]

The base image for this stage already defines node as entrypoint for the startup command, therefore we only need to specify the path to the main js file in CMD
Note the dist folder only exists in the build stage, we have copied all contents of this folder from the build stage to the current working directory /app.

title: 7  TypeScript Backend Dockerfile

7.3 Build, run, test
cd src
docker build -t fruit-backend .
docker run -p 3000:3000 -d fruit-backend
Test the endpoints in VS Code with requests.http. This needs the VS Code extension REST Client: click Send Request above a request.

title: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx
text:
8.1 Fruit Rest Client
Again we use the already known small rest client for consuming the Fruit Rest-Api from a web page.
Following adaptations in the source code have been done:
crumbs: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx

title: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx
text:
public folder added

Moved index.html into this folder
Changed tsconfig.json to generate the index.js transpilation output into this folder

package.json file added

for installing typescript compiler in the docker node image

nginx.conf file added

It overrides the default nginx configuration: every URL which does not match an existing file is answered with index.html (try_files). This is needed for single-page applications with client-side routing.
crumbs: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx

title: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx
text:
8.2 Dockerfile
The setup is again separated into two stages:

We need to use node as base image for generating the transpilation output index.js.
For the run stage, we don’t use node, but nginx as web server, which hosts both the html and javascript files => therefore we put all our application files into the common public folder. This folder will then be hosted by nginx.


8.2.1 Step 1: Build Stage
The build stage is basically the same as for the typescript backend application:
FROM node:24 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY ./package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build


8.2.2 Step 2: Run Stage
Since we have created all what nginx needs for hosting the web page into the folder /app/public in the build stage, the only thing we need to do is to copy this folder into the web root folder of nginx: /usr/share/nginx/html.
FROM nginx
COPY ./nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=builder /app/public /usr/share/nginx/html
Note:

No EXPOSE 80 or CMD required, these statements are already declared in the nginx base image.
Overriding the default.conf is only required if your web application uses client-side routing (a single-page application with several URL routes). A plain static site works with the default configuration.
crumbs: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx

title: 8  Hosting Dynamic Website with nginx
text:
8.3 Build, run, test
cd src
docker build -t fruit-frontend .
docker run -p 8888:80 -d fruit-frontend
Test the URL http://localhost:8888 in your browser.

You should see five buttons. With the backend from the previous exercise running on port 3000, GET /api/fruits shows apple,banana,peach.
Now stop the backend container and click the buttons again. Most buttons show nothing new on the page (the two .../0 buttons show fruit not found). Open the browser developer tools (F12 → tab Console) to see the real error messages.
The JavaScript code runs in your browser, not in the container. Hence it calls the backend via http://localhost:3000, and the backend container must publish port 3000 on your host.


8.3.1 Browser localhost vs. container localhost


The browser asks your computer for localhost:8888. Docker forwards this request to port 80 of the frontend container (nginx).
nginx sends back index.html and index.js. From now on, nobody in the frontend container runs this code - it runs in your browser.
When you click a button, index.js calls http://localhost:3000/api/fruits. For the browser, localhost is your computer, so the request goes to host port 3000, which Docker forwards to the backend container.
The backend answers with JSON.

Remember: localhost always means the machine (or container) where the code is running. Inside a container, localhost is the container itself. The frontend container has no backend on port 3000, so it would not help to call the backend from there.
Question: What happens if you start the backend with -p 3001:3000? What would you have to change?

title: 10  Composing a single container
text:
10.1 compose.yaml
In the container section, we have tested a docker run command for publishing a local folder through an nginx container and mapping the internal nginx port 80 to the external host port 8080:
With docker compose, we can specify such docker run configurations in a text file and use this file to start and stop (or remove) a single or multiple containers.
Refer to:
The default file name for a compose file is compose.yaml (preferred) or compose.yml. The older names docker-compose.yaml and docker-compose.yml are still supported for backwards compatibility.
Note:
Note:

title: 10  Composing a single container
text:
Older compose files often start with a version: element. It is obsolete and should be omitted.

services:

First statement is - with no indentation, starting at the very first character - the services: section, which allows to specify one or more containers (=> services) to be managed.
After this line, you need to indent with spaces (usually 2)! YAML does not allow TAB characters for indentation.

  web:

Next, we declare the service name web for the one and only container, which will be managed by this compose file.
All subsequent mappings for this service are again indented (2 more spaces)

    image: nginx

The most important service mapping is of course, on which image this container should be based.
So we define nginx with no tag, thus, the tag latest is used (which usually points to the newest stable version).



Instead of an image, which would be pulled from Docker Hub, we could also specify image build options with a build mapping, since docker compose can also involve a docker build to create the container image on the fly.
More on this later.

    ports:
      - 8080:80

A container usually represents a background server process and listens on one or more ports. These are called the container ports.
Hence, port mappings are specified in form of a list with each element started with - in a distinct row.
In our example, the nginx container port 80 is published on the host port 8080, similar to the port mapping we have done with the docker run command in the terminal.

    volumes:
      - ./wwwroot:/usr/share/nginx/html

Finally, the bind mount of a local host folder to the default nginx web root folder is configured as one element for the volumes mapping, very similar to the -v option of the docker run command.
Note that compose resolves a relative path relative to the folder of the compose file.

title: 10  Composing a single container
text:
10.2 Startup: docker compose up
If you cd into the directory, where the compose.yaml file resides, and call the docker compose up command there, you will first get following information in your terminal:

Following two steps happened:

docker compose creates a separate docker network for you.

As long as no specific docker network is configured in the compose file, this network is called <project-name>_default. The project name defaults to the name of the folder containing the compose file.
You can inspect this network with the command docker network ls, listing both the default docker networks and specific networks created manually or by means of docker compose:

bridge (where containers started manually with docker run will reside)
host and none for special network use cases
and now also the 01-compose-single-container_default network.

Note the NETWORK_ID of your new network.

docker compose started the single service as specified in the compose file for you:

We did not ask for a specific container name, hence the project name (= folder name) is used, followed by the service name web and the instance number 1.
We did not assign this container to a specific network, so it is assigned to the default network belonging to this compose file.



10.2.1 Network Inspection
You can inspect your docker network with docker network inspect <network-id>:

Here you can see following:

Network properties like the Name
IP configuration for this network including

subnet
gateway

All containers which have been assigned to this network including their IP address.

As you can see in the graphic below, a container can also be assigned to more than one docker networks:



See also:

https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/



10.2.2 Background versus Foreground
Since we started our docker compose in foreground mode, the terminal is attached to the log outputs of all containers of this compose project.
To stop the containers,

you can either press Ctrl+C in the terminal, which will stop but not remove the containers.
or you open another terminal, cd into the compose folder and type docker compose down. In this case, the containers are not only stopped, but also removed, together with the networks created by compose.



10.2.3 Background mode: docker compose up -d
To start the containers in background (detached) mode, use the -d option of the up command: docker compose up -d. Note that -d must be written after up, since it is an option of the up sub-command.
Refer to https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/

title: 11  Exercise: Compose container network
text:
11.1 Instructions
Two different web root folders are given
You shall create a file compose.yaml in this folder (next to webA and webB) for managing two nginx containers:
Hints:
Only if you are stuck: a solution is in solution/compose.yaml. Start it from this folder with docker compose -f solution/compose.yaml up -d (and stop it with docker compose -f solution/compose.yaml down).

title: 11  Exercise: Compose container network
text:
The services should be called web-1 and web-2.
The first should have the container_name webA, the second webB.
The first should be mapped to port 8081, the second to 8082.
The first should serve the folder webA (bind mount, like in the previous exercise), the second the folder webB.
Both should be assigned to a specific network called my-web-network.
This network should specify a specific IPAM config with the subnet 10.2.0.0/16



Networks are declared in a top-level networks: section, similar to services:. Look up the syntax in the compose reference: networks (see name, driver and ipam).
Each service lists the networks it belongs to in its own networks: list.
Without name:, compose would put the folder name in front of the network name.
Test: http://localhost:8081 should show the A-service, http://localhost:8082 the B-service.

title: 11  Exercise: Compose container network
text:
11.2 Expected Terminal Output

11.2.1 docker compose up -d
 - Network my-web-network  Created
 - Container webB          Started
 - Container webA          Started


11.2.2 docker ps
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE     COMMAND                  CREATED         STATUS         PORTS                                     NAMES
60d5c2755d53   nginx     "/docker-entrypoint.…"   6 minutes ago   Up 6 minutes   0.0.0.0:8082->80/tcp, [::]:8082->80/tcp   webB
c1e104106b4b   nginx     "/docker-entrypoint.…"   6 minutes ago   Up 6 minutes   0.0.0.0:8081->80/tcp, [::]:8081->80/tcp   webA



11.2.3 docker compose down
 - Container webA          Removed
 - Container webB          Removed
 - Network my-web-network  Removed

title: 11  Exercise: Compose container network
text:
11.3 Inter-Container-Communication
Both containers reside in the same user-defined bridge network, and docker provides automatic DNS resolution for such networks. This means containers inside the same network can contact each other using either their IP addresses or their host names (=> which are actually their service and/or container names)!
Note:

This DNS resolution only works in user-defined networks (like the ones created by compose). Containers in the default bridge network can only reach each other by IP address.
Refer to https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/

We can experience this by using the ping utility.

11.3.1 Execute bash in webA
We connect our terminal to the webA container with
docker exec -it webA bash
However, the ping command is not found. So we need to install it in our container:
apt update
apt install -y iputils-ping
Finally, we are able to ping orf.at and get according ping statistics.


11.3.2 ping webB
Now we can ping our neighbour container named webB and get the following output:
root@a4074b8a929b:/# ping webB
PING webB (10.2.0.2) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from webB.my-web-network (10.2.0.2): icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.066 ms
(Your IP address may be different, e.g. 10.2.0.3 - docker picks a free address from the subnet. Stop ping with Ctrl+C.)
Also working:

ping 10.2.0.2 (using the internal ip address shown in your ping output)
ping web-2 (using the service name instead of container_name)

Question: After docker compose down and docker compose up -d, is ping still installed in webA? Why (not)?

title: 12  DB Containers / Persistent Volumes
text:
12.1 Volume declaration
Especially for hosting a database container, the data managed by the DBMS should survive a container life cycle.
This means, if someone shuts down the container with docker compose down or manually removes the database container with docker rm -f ..., we would like to see the same data after launching a new database container.
For this, we need to map the file path inside the db container, where all the database files are stored internally, to a volume, which persists independently of the container.
This file path depends on the DBMS, for instance for mysql it is /var/lib/mysql
Similar to a service or network declaration, a volume declaration in a compose file looks like this:
In a terminal, the corresponding command would be docker volume create mysql-data. Compose creates the volume automatically, if it does not exist yet.
Docker-managed volumes can also be inspected and deleted manually:

title: 12  DB Containers / Persistent Volumes
text:
volumes:
  data:
    name: mysql-data



docker volume ls
docker volume inspect mysql-data
docker volume rm mysql-data (be careful!)

title: 12  DB Containers / Persistent Volumes
section: 12.2 Volume mapping for a mysql container
text:
12.2 Volume mapping for a mysql container
services:
  mysql:
    image: mysql:8.4
    container_name: dev_mysql
    environment:
      MYSQL_USER: user
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: user
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root
      MYSQL_DATABASE: userDB
    volumes:
      - data:/var/lib/mysql
With this volume mapping, the container internal path /var/lib/mysql is mapped to the docker-managed volume data (named mysql-data, according to the volume declaration above).
Note:

Still, you could map a local host path on the left side, by specifying a relative or absolute file path instead of the name of a volume.
This is called a bind mount, whereas mapping to a docker-managed volume is called a named volume.
In the first case, the files are accessible very easily, you can browse them in the local file system. But this is also more dangerous, since you could delete some files by accident.
In the second case, the files are managed by docker and stored in a part of the host file system which is managed by docker (/var/lib/docker/volumes/ on Linux, inside the Docker Desktop VM on Windows/macOS), so it is not easy at all to delete them by accident.

Refer to:

https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/ (overview of volumes, bind mounts and tmpfs mounts)
https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/

title: 12  DB Containers / Persistent Volumes
text:
12.3 phpMyAdmin
With the DNS resolution inside a docker network, a good practice for database management in docker is to hide a DBMS docker container from the external world, while only neighbour containers inside the same docker network are able to contact this DBMS.
Note:

During development, you might still want to publish the database port, so you can inspect your tables with a database tool on your host (see exercise below).

We test this security feature by setting up a second container using the phpmyadmin image, which is basically a web server providing a user interface for browsing a relational database. This web service uses PHP to communicate with the DBMS container, and for this, network traffic inside the docker network is sufficient!
Note:

That’s the reason why the mysql container does not specify a port mapping, hence it is not reachable from outside!


12.3.1 pma Container
  phpmyadmin:
    image: phpmyadmin
    container_name: dev_pma
    environment:
      PMA_HOST: mysql
      PMA_PORT: 3306
      PMA_ARBITRARY: 1
    restart: always
    ports:
      - 8183:80
During startup of a phpMyAdmin container, this application refers to several environment variables. Those can easily be specified in a compose file:

PMA_HOST: Hostname or IP address of the DBMS which shall be browsed
PMA_PORT: By default, a mysql database listens on port 3306 for incoming client connections
PMA_ARBITRARY:

If set to 0, the web interface is fixed to the given PMA_HOST. In the login dialog, you are only asked for username and password.
If set to 1, the web interface is allowed to connect to arbitrary DBMS hosts. In the login dialog, you can also enter the PMA_HOST which shall be connected, in addition to username and password.

title: 12  DB Containers / Persistent Volumes
text:
12.4 First Booting
If the compose file is started for the first time, mysql detects an empty data directory and creates the requested database and user (refer to environment variables passed to the mysql container).
Note:

These environment variables are only evaluated if the data directory is empty. Changing them later has no effect on an existing volume.

Since the docker-managed volume survives several downs and ups of the compose network, all data remain there, until someone manually deletes the volume in a terminal with docker volume rm mysql-data, or with docker compose down -v (which removes the containers together with the volumes declared in the compose file).

title: 12  DB Containers / Persistent Volumes
text:
12.5 Exercise

12.5.1 Database hidden

Boot the compose network

On the very first start, MySQL needs some time (up to about a minute) to create the database. Until then, the login fails. Watch docker logs -f dev_mysql until you see ready for connections together with port: 3306 (stop watching with Ctrl+C). An earlier line with port: 0 belongs to a temporary setup server - keep waiting.

Test the web interface in your favourite browser : http://localhost:8183

Login with root/root or user/user
Test various host names in the Server field of the login dialog: mysql (service name), dev_mysql (container name), the IP address of the container (find it with docker network inspect backend) and localhost.
Why does localhost not work? (Hint: inside the phpMyAdmin container, localhost means the phpMyAdmin container itself.)

Create a new table with some columns
Shut down the network with docker compose down.
Boot again, login to the database in the browser and inspect the new table.



12.5.2 Database with external port mapping

Try to connect to the database from an external sql browser (like JetBrains DataGrip, HeidiSQL or similar) => should not be possible.
Change the compose file and add a port mapping for the mysql container (remove the # in the commented ports lines), then run docker compose up -d again.

If you get port is already allocated, another MySQL (e.g. from XAMPP) is running on your computer. Stop it, or use another host port, e.g. 3307:3306.

Try again to connect to the database from an external sql browser => should work now! (Host localhost, port 3306, user user, password user)
Clean up: docker compose down (the volume mysql-data stays; docker compose down -v deletes it too)

Note: Passwords written directly into a compose file are fine for a local development setup, but never for a real server.

title: 13  Wordpress with docker compose
text:
13.1 First boot
This example manages three different containers in a compose file:
No networks: section is given here, so all three containers are placed in the default network of this compose project (04-wordpress-network_default). They can still reach each other by service name.

title: 13  Wordpress with docker compose
text:
Before you start: run docker compose down in the folders of the previous compose exercises. This example uses the same host ports (8080, 8183) and the same container name dev_pma.
Start with docker compose up -d.
Open http://localhost:8080. If the wordpress container is visited the first time, it will ask for an initial installation, including the database connection data.
phpMyAdmin is available at http://localhost:8183 (user wordpress, password wordpress).

title: 13  Wordpress with docker compose
text:
13.2 Exercise
Find out, how you can configure the wordpress container, so the initial installation does not ask for database connection data anymore.
Hints:

Look at the documentation of the image on Docker Hub: https://hub.docker.com/_/wordpress, section How to use this image. Look for environment variables starting with WORDPRESS_DB_.
Which values do you need? Compare with the environment section of the mysql service: host name, user, password, database name.
After changing the compose file, run docker compose up -d again. Compose recreates only the changed container.
If the page shows an error (Error establishing a database connection or HTTP 500) right after the start, the database is still starting. Wait a few seconds and reload.

Expected result: http://localhost:8080 skips the database step. After choosing the language, it directly asks for the site title, admin user name and password.
